title: Jonah sulks (Jonah 3–4)
hook: the enemy city repents and Jonah is furious that God is merciful

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jonah ran west and prayed from inside the great fish. Your line was you can't outrun him.

The fish puts Jonah out on dry land, and the word of the Lord comes a second time, exactly the same: arise, go to Ninive. This time he goes. Ninive is enormous, a three days' walk across, the text says. Jonah walks one day in and preaches a sermon of one sentence. In the Douay-Rheims: "Yet forty days, and Ninive shall be destroyed." That's all of it. No call to repent. No mention of mercy. And the city whose wickedness had come up before God believes him.
screen: `THE SAME WORD, A SECOND TIME.` → `A SERMON OF ONE SENTENCE.` → `THE CITY BELIEVES.`

segments.voice: The people proclaim a fast and put on sackcloth, from the greatest to the least. The king gets up from his throne, takes off his robe and sits in ashes. Nobody is to eat, he decrees, not even the oxen and sheep; the animals wear sackcloth too. Who knows, he says, whether God will turn and forgive. And God sees how they turned from their evil way, and doesn't bring the destruction. And Jonah is furious. He admits why he ran: I knew it. I knew you are a gracious and merciful God, patient, rich in compassion, ready to forgive. Those are God's own words about himself from Exodus, and Jonah throws them back like a complaint. He'd rather die. God asks one quiet question: do you think you have reason to be angry? He goes east of the city to watch, hoping. God makes a plant grow over him for shade, and Jonah is very glad of it. Nobody knows what plant it was. The King James says a gourd; Jerome's Latin, and so the Douay, says ivy. When Jerome's translation reached a church in North Africa, Augustine reported that the congregation nearly rioted over the change. Then a worm kills the plant, a scorching wind blows, and Jonah wants to die again. And God says: you grieve over a plant you didn't plant or grow. Should I not spare Nineveh, that great city, with more than a hundred and twenty thousand people who can't tell their right hand from their left, and many beasts? And the book ends on the question. Jonah never answers.
screen: `EVEN THE OXEN WEAR SACKCLOTH.` · `I KNEW YOU WERE MERCIFUL.` · `A GOURD, OR IVY? NOBODY KNOWS.` · `THE BOOK ENDS ON A QUESTION.` · then, large: `SHOULD I NOT SPARE NINEVEH?`

segments.voice: Think of someone who got a second chance you're not sure they deserved: a sibling who always gets forgiven, a colleague who messed up and got promoted anyway. Notice the sulk, if there is one, the part of you sitting east of the city hoping for fire, and let God's question sit beside it: should I not spare them? Then see if you can be glad, even a little. If you pray, pray for them by name.
Jonah sulks. The prophet whose one-sentence sermon saved an enemy city, and who sat outside it, angry that God was merciful. Today's word.
Your line: should I not spare them. The question is still open. Four hundred thirty days now.

howItsDone: Catholics hear Nineveh's repentance read at Mass in Lent, and the Church holds up the Ninevites' fasting and sackcloth as a picture of the penance of the Lenten season.

fork.setup: you're Jonah. you preached destruction, and the whole enemy city repented. God spared them. what do you do?
options: throw a party with the Ninevites.
get angry, and sit outside the city hoping it burns anyway.
fork.reveal: he's furious, and says why he ran: he knew God was gracious and merciful. he sits east of the city to watch.

original.note: Hebrew: Jonah's plant. nobody knows what it was; translations have gourd, ivy or castor-oil plant.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jonah's story ends when the fish spits him out.
what it means: the second half is the harder story: a prophet angry that God forgave his enemies, and God asking him to care.
what a scholar hears: Jonah quotes God's self-description from Exodus 34:6 as a complaint; and the book ends on an unanswered question, aimed at the reader.
guess: a prophet angry that God showed mercy
a prophet sad his warning went unheard
a prophet grieving the city's destruction

chat.says: Why was Jonah angry when Nineveh was spared?
options: He knew God was merciful and ready to forgive, and he didn't want the city spared.
The city's fast was fake, and he could see they hadn't really changed.
He feared the king would punish him for his harsh one-sentence sermon.
chat.meaning: Jonah admits it: I knew you are gracious and merciful, ready to forgive. He'd rather see fire, and God asks, should I not spare Nineveh?

sackcloth.meaning: rough cloth worn to show grief and repentance

Exodus.meaning: the Bible book of the escape from Egypt

Jerome.meaning: the scholar who translated the Bible into Latin

Nineveh.meaning: a great city of the Assyrians
